LESSONS.title: Getting data ready
LESSONS.goal: Make a name list and a value list for a chart
summary: Pair a name list with a value list
Items at the same index go together
Split a dictionary with keys and values

cards.say: To draw a chart, first get the data ready. Make a name list and a value list separately, so items at the same index go together. Jan sits at index 0.
cards.code:
months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]
spend = [30000, 12000, 45000]
for i in range(len(months)):
    print(months[i], spend[i])

cards.say: If your data is in a dictionary, keys and values split it into a name list and a value list easily. They keep the order you added things in.
cards.code:
d = {"Jan": 30000, "Feb": 12000}
names = list(d.keys())
values = list(d.values())
print(names, values)

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
names = ["bread", "milk"]
vals = [2, 5]
print(vals[1])
items.explain: Names and values pair up by index. Index 1 is the second slot, so the value is 5, and its partner name is milk.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
d = {"a": 3, "b": 7}
print(list(d.values()))
items.explain: values takes out only the dictionary's values, in the order they were added. The one that takes out the names (keys) is keys.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
names = ["a", "b", "c"]
vals = [4, 6]
print(len(names) == len(vals))
items.explain: There are 3 names but only 2 values, so the counts differ. A chart can't be drawn when they differ, so you can check with len first.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the total, 10, is printed.
items.code:
spend = [3, 5, 2]
total = ___(spend)
print(total)
items.explain: sum adds up every value in the list to get 10. max gives the biggest, 5, and len gives the number of slots, 3.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the total 10 prints, then Done.
items.explain: The list must exist before sum can add it, and the total must exist before you can print it. Done prints once, at the very end.

items.task: One line from input() (leave the parentheses empty) holds monthly spending, separated by spaces. Use split() and for to make a list of numbers, print “Month 1: amount” line by line, then “Total: N” with sum at the end. Example: 5000 2000 gives Month 1: 5000, Month 2: 2000, Total: 7000

tests.expect:
Month 1: 0
Month 2: 700
Month 3: 0
Month 4: 300
Month 5: 100
Total: 1100

hints: You don't know how many amounts will come in. It has to work for 1 amount and for 5.
split() cuts one line into a list of pieces. The pieces are strings, so turn them into int before adding.
Collect the numbers in an empty list with append, then loop with index i; the month is i + 1. sum comes last.

values = []
for s in line.split():
    values.append(int(s))
for i in range(len(___)):
    m = i + 1
    print(f"Month {m}: {values[i]}")
(print the total at the end)
items.solution:
line = input()
values = []
for s in line.split():
    values.append(int(s))
for i in range(len(values)):
    m = i + 1
    print(f"Month {m}: {values[i]}")
print(f"Total: {sum(values)}")
items.explain: range(len(values)) loops over any number of inputs, and the month is i + 1. It works even when there's only one amount.

items.q: What must the two lists for a chart have?
items.explain: One name pairs with one value, so both lists need the same length. The count and the contents can be anything.

LESSONS.title: Bar charts
LESSONS.goal: Draw a bar chart with chart.bar
summary: import chart brings in the drawing tool
chart.bar(names, values)
chart.show() at the end shows it

cards.say: Now let's draw! import chart brings in the tool. Give chart.bar a name list and a value list, in that order, and you get bars. Great for comparing items. Call chart.show() at the end to see it.
cards.code:
import chart
names = ["apple", "pear", "orange"]
sales = [7, 4, 9]
chart.bar(names, sales)
chart.show()

cards.say: You can chart values from input too. Turn them into numbers, collect them in a list, and hand it to bar. If the names and values don't match in count, you get a ValueError clue.
cards.code:
import chart
names = ["apple", "pear", "orange"]
sales = []
for s in input().split():
    sales.append(int(s))
chart.bar(names, sales)
chart.show()
print(sum(sales))

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
v = [3, 8, 5]
chart.bar(["A", "B", "C"], v)
chart.show()
print(max(v))
items.explain: The chart draws three bars, and print shows the biggest value, 8. B is the name for 8, but print shows the value.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.code:
import chart
chart.bar(["A", "B"], [1, 2, 3])
chart.show()
items.explain: There are 2 names but 3 values, so they don't pair up. When that happens, chart.bar gives a ValueError clue.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
chart.bar(["A"], [5])
print("Chart done")
items.explain: chart.show() is never called, so no chart appears. Only the printed text, Chart done, shows up.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the chart shows up.
items.code:
import chart
chart.bar(["A", "B"], [4, 6])
chart.___()
print("Done")
items.explain: The command that sends the chart to the screen is show. bar and xlabel need something inside the parentheses, so empty ones give a TypeError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the bar chart shows up.
items.explain: Bring in the tool with import, draw bars with bar, then show them at the end. Calling show when there's no chart to draw gives a ValueError.

items.task: One line from input() (leave the parentheses empty) holds 3 sales counts: apple, pear, orange. Use split() and for to make a list of numbers, give it to chart.bar with the names, and call chart.show(). Print the total with sum as “Total: N”. Example: 7 4 9 gives Total: 20
hints: The sales counts change with every input. The bar heights must change with the input too.
Like 17-1, cut the line with split, turn the pieces into int and collect them in a list. The name list is apple, pear, orange.
Give chart.bar the name list and the value list in that order, then call chart.show() at the end.

names = ["apple", "pear", "orange"]
sales = []
for s in input().split():
    sales.append(int(s))
chart.bar(names, ___)
(then show and print the total)
items.solution:
import chart
names = ["apple", "pear", "orange"]
sales = []
for s in input().split():
    sales.append(int(s))
chart.bar(names, sales)
chart.show()
print(f"Total: {sum(sales)}")
items.explain: The input sets the bar heights, and calling show brings up the chart. Even the edge case of all zeros draws fine.

items.q: In chart.bar(names, values), what does values do?
items.explain: names go under the bars, and values are the bar heights. You'll add a title separately in 17-4.

LESSONS.title: Line charts
LESSONS.goal: Draw changes over time with chart.line
summary: Changes over time: chart.line
Used just like bar
Call show to see the chart

cards.say: For values that change over time, like temperature, a line chart works best. chart.line also takes a name list and a value list, and show displays it. It's used just like bar.
cards.code:
import chart
days = "Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri".split()
temps = [18, 21, 15, 17, 20]
chart.line(days, temps)
chart.show()

cards.say: The ups and downs are joined into one line. You can print the highest and lowest values with max and min too.
cards.code:
import chart
days = "Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri".split()
temps = [18, 21, 15, 17, 20]
chart.line(days, temps)
chart.show()
print(max(temps), min(temps))

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
t = [18, 21, 15]
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"], t)
chart.show()
print(max(t) - min(t))
items.explain: The highest, 21, minus the lowest, 15, is 6. The chart shows a line going up and down.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
t = []
for s in "4 -3 0".split():
    t.append(int(s))
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"], t)
chart.show()
print(min(t))
items.explain: You can chart values below zero too. min finds the smallest value, -3. That's Tuesday, where the line dips below 0.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue"], [5, 5])
print("Line done")
items.explain: Without show, the line doesn't appear. Like bar, line needs chart.show() called at the end.

items.q: Fill in the blank so a line chart is drawn.
items.code:
import chart
chart.___(["Mon", "Tue"], [3, 6])
chart.show()
print("Done")
items.explain: A line chart is line. bar draws bars, so the chart changes, and show can't take names and values, so it's a TypeError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the line chart shows up.
items.explain: The order is import, line, show. Calling show before drawing the line gives a ValueError saying there's no chart to draw.

items.task: One line from input() (leave the parentheses empty) holds 5 temperatures, Mon to Fri. Use split() and for to make a list of numbers, give it to chart.line with the day names, and call chart.show(). Print “High: N” with max. Example: 18 21 15 17 20 gives High: 21
hints: The temperatures change with every input. Some weeks are below zero, and some have the same temperature every day.
Same flow as 17-2: split the line, turn the pieces into int and make a list. This time it's line.
Give chart.line the Mon–Fri day list and the temperature list, then show it. The high is max.

days = "Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri".split()
temps = []
(collect the input here)
chart.line(days, ___)
(then show and print the high)
items.solution:
import chart
days = "Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri".split()
temps = []
for s in input().split():
    temps.append(int(s))
chart.line(days, temps)
chart.show()
print(f"High: {max(temps)}")
items.explain: max simply finds the biggest value, so even a week of only sub-zero days correctly gives -1. The line follows the input neatly.

items.q: Which chart shows temperature changes over time well?
items.explain: Trends and ups and downs show up well when joined by a line. Bars work too, but a line chart is more natural for seeing change.

LESSONS.title: Labeling charts
LESSONS.goal: Add a title and axis labels to a chart
summary: chart.title adds a title
chart.xlabel: across, ylabel: up
Call them all before show

cards.say: A bare chart can be hard to read. Add a title with chart.title, the x-axis (across) label with xlabel, and the y-axis (up) label with ylabel. Call them all before show.
cards.code:
import chart
names = ["apple", "pear", "orange"]
sales = [7, 4, 9]
chart.bar(names, sales)
chart.title("Fruit Sales")
chart.xlabel("Fruit")
chart.ylabel("Count")
chart.show()

cards.say: A title is a string, so you can build it from a variable or from input. This code uses one line of input as the title.
cards.code:
import chart
name = input()
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue"], [3, 5])
chart.title(name)
chart.show()

items.q: Which command labels the x-axis (along the bottom)?
items.explain: xlabel is the x-axis (across), and ylabel is the y-axis (up). title is the heading at the very top.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
t = "Score" + " Chart"
chart.bar(["A", "B"], [80, 90])
chart.title(t)
chart.show()
print(t)
items.explain: A title is a string too, so you can join it with +. Score Chart goes on top of the chart, and print shows the same text.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
chart.bar(["A"], [1])
chart.title("Title")
print("Done")
items.explain: title alone doesn't bring up a chart. Call the labeling commands before show, and show must come at the end.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the y-axis says “Count”.
items.code:
import chart
chart.bar(["A", "B"], [4, 6])
chart.___("Count")
chart.show()
print("Done")
items.explain: The y-axis (up) is ylabel. xlabel would put it on the x-axis and title at the very top, so the chart would change.

items.q: Put the lines in order so “Fruit name” prints, then Done.
items.explain: An axis label is a string too, so you can join it with +. Print label after joining, and Done goes last.

items.task: Two lines of input() (leave the parentheses empty): a title, then 3 sales counts for apple, pear, orange. Collect the numbers with split() and for, draw chart.bar, set title to the title, xlabel “Fruit”, ylabel “Count”, then show. Print “Max: N” with max. Example: 7 4 9 gives Max: 9
hints: The title and the sales change with every input. Don't type the title text in directly.
You drew bars in 17-2 and just learned title, xlabel and ylabel. Call them all before show.
Give chart.title the first input line, title, and give the axes the fixed text “Fruit” and “Count”.

chart.bar(names, sales)
chart.title(___)
chart.xlabel("Fruit")
chart.ylabel("Count")
chart.show()
(then print the max)
items.solution:
import chart
title = input()
names = ["apple", "pear", "orange"]
sales = []
for s in input().split():
    sales.append(int(s))
chart.bar(names, sales)
chart.title(title)
chart.xlabel("Fruit")
chart.ylabel("Count")
chart.show()
print(f"Max: {max(sales)}")
items.explain: The title comes from the input, so each chart gets its own title. With axis labels too, you can tell what the chart is about at a glance.

items.q: Where should chart.title, xlabel and ylabel be called?
items.explain: show sends the chart out, so label it before that. Labels added after show don't reach the chart that's already out.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 17 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Collect data, calculate, and draw it as a chart
summary: Lists first, then math, then the chart
bar compares, line shows change
Finish with title, axis labels, show

cards.say: Let's wrap up Chapter 17. Get the name and value lists ready, pick a chart, add a title and axis labels, then show it. That flow is all there is to data visualization.
cards.code:
import chart
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
mins = [30, 60, 45]
chart.line(days, mins)
chart.title("Study Time")
chart.xlabel("Day")
chart.ylabel("Minutes")
chart.show()

cards.say: In real projects, people use matplotlib. To move the chart above over to it, chart becomes plt, and only line changes to plot. bar, title, xlabel, ylabel and show keep their names. English labels work as is; Korean text needs a font setting.
cards.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
mins = [30, 60, 45]
plt.plot(days, mins)
plt.title("Study Time")
plt.xlabel("Day")
plt.ylabel("Minutes")
plt.show()

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
d = {"Mon": 30, "Tue": 50}
print(sum(d.values()))
items.explain: values takes out 30 and 50, and sum adds them to 80. The one that takes out the names is keys.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
s = [4, 9, 6]
chart.bar(["A", "B", "C"], s)
chart.show()
print(sum(s))
items.explain: The chart draws three bars, and print shows all the values added up, 19. 9 is just the biggest value.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
t = [12, 8, 10]
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"], t)
chart.show()
print(min(t))
items.explain: The line dips lowest on Tuesday. min finds that value, 8.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the x-axis says “Day”.
items.code:
import chart
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue"], [3, 6])
chart.___("Day")
chart.show()
print("Done")
items.explain: The x-axis (across) is xlabel. ylabel puts text on the y-axis and title at the very top, so the chart would change.

items.task: One line from input() (leave the parentheses empty) holds 7 study times in minutes, Mon to Sun. Print “Total: N min”, “Average: N min” (int, drop decimals) and “Top day: Sat” (on a tie, the earlier day) with sum and max. Draw chart.line by day with title “My Study Log”, x “Day”, y “Minutes”, then show. Example: 60 0 45 90 30 120 15 gives Total: 360 min

tests.expect:
Total: 360 min
Average: 51 min
Top day: Sat

Total: 0 min
Average: 0 min
Top day: Mon

Total: 211 min
Average: 30 min
Top day: Sun

Total: 200 min
Average: 28 min
Top day: Tue

hints: Study times change with every input. Some weeks are all 0s, and sometimes the top day is the first or last day.
Use all of Chapter 17. Collect with split, calculate with sum and max, then draw with line, labels and show.
For the top day, find the slot where the max value first appears and take the day at that index. The average is int(total / 7).

total = sum(values)
top = values.index(max(values))
avg = int(total / ___)
print(f"Average: {avg} min")
(print the total and the day; chart: line→title→xlabel→ylabel→show)
items.solution:
import chart
week = "Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat Sun"
days = week.split()
values = []
for s in input().split():
    values.append(int(s))
total = sum(values)
top = values.index(max(values))
print(f"Total: {total} min")
avg = int(total / 7)
print(f"Average: {avg} min")
day = days[top]
print(f"Top day: {day}")
chart.line(days, values)
chart.title("My Study Log")
chart.xlabel("Day")
chart.ylabel("Minutes")
chart.show()
items.explain: Both the math and the chart follow the input. All zeros and tied values work too, and every Chapter 17 tool came together in one program. Amazing work!

items.q: What's the right flow for chart code?
items.explain: The lists to draw come first, and labels go before show. And congratulations! You started from one print line and made it all the way to charts. Now collect your own data and draw it. I'm always cheering for you.

ADVANCED.title: Layering lines
ADVANCED.goal: Draw several lines layered in one chart
summary: Call line again with the same names
chart.legend labels each line
Call show just once, at the end

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. Call line twice with the same names and the two lines overlap. Give legend the names in the order you drew them. Call show just once.
cards.code:
import chart
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
a = [3, 5, 4]
b = [1, 2, 6]
chart.line(days, a)
chart.line(days, b)
chart.legend(["Minji", "Jun"])
chart.title("Study Time")
chart.show()

cards.say: matplotlib on a real computer works much the same. Call plt.plot twice and give plt.legend the names. Here, chart can layer up to 3 lines.
cards.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
a = [3, 5, 4]
b = [1, 2, 6]
plt.plot(days, a)
plt.plot(days, b)
plt.legend(["Minji", "Jun"])
plt.show()

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
a = [2, 4]
b = [5, 1]
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue"], a)
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue"], b)
chart.show()
print(max(a) + max(b))
items.explain: Two lines are drawn layered in one chart. print adds a's biggest value, 4, and b's biggest, 5, to get 9.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.code:
import chart
chart.line(["Mon"], [1])
chart.line(["Mon"], [2])
chart.legend(["Minji"])
chart.show()
items.explain: There are 2 lines but only 1 name, so they don't pair up. legend needs as many names as there are lines.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.code:
import chart
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue"], [1, 2])
chart.line(["Mon", "Wed"], [3, 4])
chart.show()
items.explain: A layered line needs the same x-axis names as the first line. The second line's names differ, so you get a ValueError clue.

items.q: Fill in the blank so each line gets a label.
items.code:
import chart
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue"], [3, 6])
chart.line(["Mon", "Tue"], [4, 1])
chart.___(["Minji", "Jun"])
chart.show()
items.explain: Line labels come from legend. title and xlabel take a single string, so giving them a list of names gives a TypeError clue.

items.q: Put the lines in order so two layered lines appear.
items.explain: Draw both lines first, then call show once. The order you draw them in is the order of the lines in the chart.

items.task: Two lines of input() (leave the parentheses empty): Minji's and Jun's study minutes, 5 each for Mon to Fri. Make two lists with split() and for, call line twice, then legend(["Minji", "Jun"]), title "Study Time", and show. Print “Minji studied more” or “Jun studied more” for the bigger sum, or “Same” on a tie. Example: sums 10 and 8 give Minji studied more
hints: The study minutes change with every input. Sometimes both totals are the same.
Call 17-3's line twice and label the lines with the legend you just learned. Collecting input is the same as in 17-1.
Make lists a and b, call line with a then b, and give legend the names Minji then Jun. Compare the totals with sum.

chart.line(days, a)
chart.line(days, ___)
chart.legend(["Minji", "Jun"])
(then title and show, and compare with if/elif/else)
items.solution:
import chart
days = "Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri".split()
a = []
for s in input().split():
    a.append(int(s))
b = []
for s in input().split():
    b.append(int(s))
chart.line(days, a)
chart.line(days, b)
chart.legend(["Minji", "Jun"])
chart.title("Study Time")
chart.show()
if sum(a) > sum(b):
    print("Minji studied more")
elif sum(a) < sum(b):
    print("Jun studied more")
else:
    print("Same")
items.explain: Both lines follow the input in one chart, and the labels are in the right order. Catching the tie with else was a careful touch, too.

items.q: In chart.legend(["A", "B"]), what order are the names in?
options: The order the lines were drawn
items.explain: The line from the first chart.line call gets the first name. Call legend after drawing all the lines. Real matplotlib needs that order too for the labels to land right.

ADVANCED.title: Pick, then draw
ADVANCED.goal: Pick items that match, sort them, and draw them
summary: Filter with range(len) + if + append
Sort biggest-first with def and key=
a[:3] keeps just the first three

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. Let's do 7-3's filtering on two lists at once, names and values. Check the condition at the same index i, and append each pair that passes to both lists.
cards.code:
import chart
names = "latte mocha tea soda".split()
sales = [5, 2, 8, 1]
big_n = []
big_v = []
for i in range(len(names)):
    if sales[i] >= 3:
        big_n.append(names[i])
        big_v.append(sales[i])
chart.bar(big_n, big_v)
chart.show()
print(big_n)

cards.say: To sort most-sold first, pass a def function to key= like in 9-3. Then slice the sorted list with rank[:2] like in 7-4 to keep just the first two.
cards.code:
def get_n(pair):
    return pair[1]

pairs = [
    ("latte", 5),
    ("tea", 8),
    ("mocha", 2),
]
rank = sorted(
    pairs,
    key=get_n,
    reverse=True,
)
top = rank[:2]
names = []
vals = []
for name, n in top:
    names.append(name)
    vals.append(n)
print(names, vals)

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
a = ["x", "y", "z"]
v = [4, 9, 6]
keep = []
for i in range(len(a)):
    if v[i] > 5:
        keep.append(a[i])
print(keep)
items.explain: Only indexes 1 and 2 have values over 5. What gets collected is the name at that index, a[i], not the value, so it's y and z.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import chart
names = ["a", "b", "c"]
score = [60, 59, 80]
ok_n = []
ok_v = []
for i in range(len(names)):
    if score[i] >= 60:
        ok_n.append(names[i])
        ok_v.append(score[i])
chart.bar(ok_n, ok_v)
chart.show()
print(len(ok_n))
items.explain: Exactly 60 still passes >= 60; only the 59 drops out. Only the two that passed are drawn, and len is 2.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
rank = [9, 7, 4, 2]
print(rank[:3])
items.explain: [:3] cuts the first 3 into a new list. Those are slots 0, 1 and 2: 9, 7, 4.

items.q: Fill in the key= blank so it sorts by value.
items.explain: key= takes just the function name, no parentheses. get_n(d) calls it right there and causes an error, and p is a name that doesn't exist here.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the two biggest values, [9, 6], print.
items.explain: Sort biggest-first, then cut the first two. If you cut first, you get [4, 9] and miss the biggest values.

items.task: Three lines of input() (leave the parentheses empty): menu names, sales counts (space-separated), and a limit. Pick those at or above the limit with range(len) and if, sort most-first with def and key=, slice the first 3, draw chart.bar (title "Popular Menu"), and print “Picked: N” (how many you picked). Example: limit 5 with latte 8, tea 3, mocha 5 gives Picked: 2
hints: Both the menu and the limit change with every input. A count exactly equal to the limit counts too.
Do 7-3's filtering on both names and counts, and sort with a def function passed to key= like in 9-3. Slicing is 7-4's [:3].
Bundle each passing pair as (name, count) into pairs, sort, cut with [:3], then use for to make a name list and a value list and draw them.
items.solution:
import chart
nm = input().split()
cnt = []
for s in input().split():

Group and add by week and by activity
Summarize with 2 charts and text

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. Drawing all 31 days as they are gives too many points. (day - 1) // 7 turns days 1–7 into 0 and days 8–14 into 1, so you can use it as a week index.
Read the log CSV, add the minutes into each week's slot, and add up totals by activity in a dictionary. Draw two charts and summarize in text too. One run can show up to 3 charts.
cards.code:
import csv
import chart
weeks = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
kinds = {}
f = open("log.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    w = (int(row[0]) - 1) // 7
    n = int(row[2])
    weeks[w] = weeks[w] + n
    k = row[1]
    kinds[k] = kinds.get(k, 0) + n
f.close()
labels = "W1 W2 W3 W4 W5".split()
chart.line(labels, weeks)
chart.show()
names = list(kinds.keys())
vals = list(kinds.values())
chart.bar(names, vals)
chart.show()
print("Total:", sum(weeks))

items.solution:
import csv
import chart
weeks = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
kinds = {}
f = open("log.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    w = (int(row[0]) - 1) // 7
    n = int(row[2])
    weeks[w] = weeks[w] + n
    k = row[1]
    kinds[k] = kinds.get(k, 0) + n
f.close()
labels = "W1 W2 W3 W4 W5".split()
chart.line(labels, weeks)
chart.title("Time by Week")
chart.show()
names = list(kinds.keys())
vals = list(kinds.values())
chart.bar(names, vals)
chart.title("Time by Activity")
chart.show()
print(f"Total: {sum(weeks)} min")
top_w = weeks.index(max(weeks)) + 1
print(f"Busiest week: {top_w}")
top_k = names[vals.index(max(vals))]
print(f"Top activity: {top_k}")
items.explain: You grouped 31 days into 5 week slots and a few activity slots to cut the points, and both charts and the text come from the same totals. The day 7/8 boundary and ties work too.
